# Conclusion {#sec-chapter6}

The three research questions posed at the outset each have a direct answer. This chapter states those answers, reflects on their limits and identifies what future work needs to address.

## Research Summary

This study set out to close a specific gap. Vendor-dominated trading IT lacked a quantitative, service-level instrument for prioritising TD, since code-centric tools cannot operate where source code is inaccessible. Following a Design Science approach [@hevnerDesignScienceInformation2004], five operational indicators were derived from the literature, mapped to TD dimensions (@tbl-indicators-lit), then operationalised from two years of live ITSM and CMDB records at a regulated Swiss financial institution. A TOPSIS model ranked six production services under two weight configurations and two observation years. The evaluation in @sec-chapter5 tested the ranking from five directions, from weight sensitivity across the entire weight space to structural rigour under service removal. The artefact works in the sense the pragmatist stance of @sec-chapter3 demands, producing a defensible, reproducible ordering from data the organisation already holds.

## Findings Against Research Questions

**RQ1** asked how TD can be prioritised quantitatively at the service level from operational data. The framework itself is the answer. Five indicators, three from ITSM and two from the CMDB, feed a TOPSIS model that orders services by debt priority without any recourse to source code. Its multi-criteria form is not decorative. The ranking diverges from an incident-only view ($\tau = 0.733$ in 2025, $0.200$ in 2024), a divergence that was not guaranteed and would have collapsed had the indicators moved together. SVC-01 rises from fourth to third on infrastructure and patch debt an incident count ignores, while SVC-05 falls on a clean infrastructure profile.

**RQ2** asked to what extent operational metrics serve as valid proxies for TD severity. To a demonstrable but bounded extent. Each indicator's link to a debt dimension is inherited from the literature (@tbl-indicators-lit) rather than established here. What this study adds is evidence that the composite behaves as an instrument should. The ranked profiles are differentiated rather than one deficiency in disguise. SVC-06 carries severe debt across dimensions, SVC-01 quieter structural exposure behind a moderate incident record, SVC-04 the reverse, SVC-03 neither. No single indicator reproduces the ordering. This is a necessary condition for the proxy claim, not a sufficient one: criterion validity cannot be established, since no independent measure of non-code debt exists to validate against. The proxy relationship therefore remains what @sec-chapter1 called it, a proposition that survived every test this design allows, not an established law.

**RQ3** asked how stable the rankings are under weight perturbation. Stable at both extremes, concentrated but weight-dependent at the top. The two configurations agree closely in 2025 ($\tau = 0.867$), and across 20,000 Monte Carlo weightings SVC-03 is last in 96.4% and SVC-06 first in 65.1%, otherwise ceding rank 1 only to SVC-04 or SVC-01. The top is thus dominated by SVC-06 within a stable three-service cluster while the lowest priority is weight-invariant. The 2024 profiles are more compressed, dividing the high-priority ranks more evenly (@sec-absolutemode) and marking the line between what the framework settles and what remains a managerial judgement.

## Theoretical and Methodological Contribution

The contribution to knowledge is threefold, and distinct from the practical contribution in @sec-practicalcontribution. Empirically, to the best of current knowledge, this is the first application of TOPSIS to live ITSM and CMDB records for TD prioritisation in financial trading IT. It addresses the absence of validated quantitative approaches that @lenarduzziSystematicLiteratureReview2021 identified across the field. Conceptually, the study contributes an operationally defined indicator set with an explicit literature mapping to debt dimensions, with evidence on how the set behaves under evaluation. Methodologically, and less anticipated, the evaluation produced a finding of independent interest. VIKOR's regret and the absolute-mode variant both refuse to reward a merely sample-extreme service the way vector-normalised TOPSIS does, and the 2024 data show this difference reordering the high-priority services. The resulting division of labour is a transferable design lesson beyond this case.

## Practical Contribution {#sec-practicalcontribution}

For the case organisation and similar institutions, the framework converts data already held in routine ITSM and CMDB records into an auditable priority ordering. Its primary use is portfolio oversight. Services are currently assessed one at a time, by different teams and on different evidence, so no consistent view of debt-related status exists across the portfolio. The ranking supplies one, and the profiles behind it show why each service sits where it does, letting portfolio managers and senior management argue remediation budgets and vendor conversations from a common picture rather than competing anecdotes. It also surfaces the debt current governance is most likely to miss. SVC-06 combines a heavy incident load with the portfolio's worst lifecycle and patch position, while SVC-01 looks comparatively quiet on incidents yet carries the highest MTTR and substantial infrastructure-lifecycle exposure once that exposure is measured per component rather than in aggregate.

The regulatory relevance is narrower than compliance. FINMA Circular 2023/1 places ICT risk management under board-level oversight [@finmaCircular202312024], and unsupported components and patch delay are ICT risks in that sense. The framework was not designed against the circular. However, it provides a holistic overview of some of the exposures the institution must oversee in any case.

The framework is also transparent and reproducible by construction. Indicator definitions, normalisation, weights and computation are stated in full, with the implementation in @sec-appendixa and the input data in @sec-appendixb. Any reported ranking can be recomputed and independently verified. Proprietary static analysis tools, by contrast, rest on rulesets that users cannot inspect and that disagree on the same codebase [@amanatidisEvaluatingAgreementTechnical2020]. In a regulated setting, a verifiable ranking is easier to defend before auditors than an opaque score.

Two conditions govern its use. The scores are ordinal decision-support signals, not measurements of debt. They also describe services, not teams, since high-debt profiles typically reflect historical design decisions rather than current custodians [@ahmadTechnicalDebtNot2026].

## Limitations and Future Work

The limitations in @sec-datalimitations and @sec-evaluationlimitations frame what remains to be done. The six-service demonstration set, selected for data completeness, limits the power of the rank-correlation tests and shares its dataset with the framework's construction, so the evaluation establishes robustness and method-independence rather than criterion validity. The design is cross-sectional. The CFR indicator shares its incident numerator with incident frequency, and recording-practice variation across teams can compress scores where informal incident handling is common. The method disagreement over the single top rank, documented in @sec-convergent and @sec-absolutemode, adds a further boundary. The single top rank is dominated by SVC-06 but weight-dependent within the SVC-01, SVC-04 and SVC-06 cluster across the weight space, a compensability judgement between concentrated structural exposure and diffuse operational debt. The framework informs that judgement rather than settles it.

Four directions follow, each addressing a limitation above. The first is external validation: replicating the framework at two or three further regulated institutions and comparing their indicator weights and dimension mappings, to test the proxy proposition beyond this case. The second is longitudinal evaluation: tracking with a lagged design whether high-priority services later generate the consequences the debt literature predicts [@bankerTechnicalDebtFirm2020], the route to the criterion validity this design cannot reach. The third is portfolio-wide deployment once indicator coverage is complete, replacing the demonstration set with a live ranking and, because Kendall's $\tau$ gains power with sample size, strengthening the stability tests. The fourth is deriving the absolute-mode bounds from regulatory or cross-industry end-of-support benchmarks rather than organisational thresholds, making scores comparable between organisations as well as between years.

## Reflective Note

Two aspects of this study turned out differently from what I expected. I anticipated that the main difficulty would be computational. It was instead definitional. Deciding what an incident count or a derived change failure rate can legitimately mean consumed more effort than implementing the model. I also expected the alternative methods to be a simple confirmation exercise. Instead, their disagreement over SVC-06 became one of the more instructive results, forcing an explicit position on whether debt dimensions are compensatory. The discipline of Design Science helped in both cases, by keeping the study honest about the difference between what the artefact demonstrates and what it merely suggests. The framework does not measure TD. It orders services by the operational shadow debt casts, and within the limits stated above, it does so reproducibly, defensibly and in a form a regulated institution can act on. Its wider significance is to show that the operational data enterprises already hold can prioritise technical debt where source code cannot be reached, giving vendor-dominated, regulated institutions a defensible basis for ICT-risk decisions they must make regardless.
